definition: Colossus means a gigantic statue or thing.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word colossus. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know colossus should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Cut into the canyon wall, the sandstone colossus watched over the trade road for twelve centuries, its knees alone taller than the caravans passing beneath.
A statue can be any size at all — a garden gnome qualifies — while a colossus is defined by overwhelming scale.

A monument is built big enough to honor its subject, yet even a grand one stays within human measure; a colossus bursts past it, so vast that visitors gauge it in stories and ship-masts — which is why this ladder can end nowhere else.

A titan is a towering figure of power — a titan of industry, a tech titan. Borrowed from mythic giants, the word points at influence first and size second, and a titan is a person or force, never an object you could carve or cast. A colossus is, first of all, physically gigantic.

A monolith is a single huge block of stone — or an organization so massive and uniform it seems carved from one. Either way it is one solid, faceless mass. A colossus is a shaped figure: gigantic, but sculpted into a form people crane their necks to take in.

Colossus means a gigantic statue or thing.
When the dictator fell, the crowds went first to the steel colossus of him in Victory Square.
It took three cranes and two days to bring the hundred-foot figure down, and its severed head, big as a delivery van, sat in the grass all winter.

Colossus outdoes 'statue' and even 'monument' by making size the whole point: from the Colossus of Rhodes onward, it names a figure so gigantic that people measure it in ship-masts and stories — and, by extension, any towering giant of its field.
Colossus is the word when size itself inspires awe: a carved colossus, or a person or company that towers over a field like one.
Its unit-mate behemoth looms with menace, a monster crowding everything near it; a colossus stands magnificent, a marvel to look up at.
For a giant of myth-level influence, titan is the close cousin.

For four centuries the islanders plowed around what they took for a granite ridge in the barley field.
Then a drought shrank the topsoil, and the 'ridge' showed a wrist, then fingers longer than fence posts.
Archaeologists uncovered a fallen colossus of a forgotten king, toppled face-down in some ancient quake: a single carved figure longer than the village's main street.
Raising it was debated for a decade; in the end the islanders left the king where he lay and built a walkway over him instead.
Schoolchildren now cross the royal shoulders each morning, and visitors pay to stand in the cupped stone palm.
